items.text:
Scientists tell Commons exposure to colibactin in early life is potential driver of early-onset colorectal cancer
Exposure to a bacterial toxin in early life has emerged as a leading suspect in the rise of bowel cancer among those under 50, MPs have heard.
Cases of early-onset bowel cancer have doubled in many countries in the past two decades, and while rising obesity and a fall in physical activity are contributors, researchers believe other factors must also be involved.
Dr Karl Smith-Byrne, a senior molecular epidemiologist at the University of Oxford, told the Commons science and technology committee that known risk factors for colorectal cancer, such as obesity, smoking and alcohol, can explain only about half of the cases doctors diagnose.
He said he did not find it “plausible” that the rise in early onset bowel cancer could be entirely explained by risk factors that researchers were already aware of.
Last year scientists identified a toxin called colibactin, produced by some variants of E coli bacteria in the gut, as a potential driver of early onset colorectal cancer. Hallmark mutations caused by the toxin were three times more common in tumours from people under 40 than in those from people over 70.
More work is needed to understand whether colibactin actually drives bowel cancer, but it is a question scientists are now actively pursuing. “That’s probably the leading explanation at the moment,” Smith-Byrne told MPs.
Prof Mike Stratton at the Sanger Institute, who was not at the hearing, has said that colibactin causes mutations in some children but not others, with evidence of mutations appearing as early as infancy. By the age of 10, affected children can have a similar “mutational burden” to a 50-year-old, his work showed.
“If it is causing mutations, it’s causing mutations at a sensitive period earlier in life, and that can give that person’s colon or their rectum a head start on its journey towards being cancerous or developing these tumours,” said Smith-Byrne, who is himself a survivor of early-onset rectal cancer.
Some suspect that particular variants of E coli that normally live harmlessly in the gut have evolved in recent decades to produce colibactin. Prof Elio Riboli, a cancer epidemiologist at Imperial College London, told the committee: “This colibactin is essentially found in people born after 1960. Something has happened in the E coli bacteria … There must have been a mutation, and there is a new bacteria.”

items.title: Medieval Readers Saw Floods, Plagues and Comets as Omens of Doom—So They Created a Mysterious Manuscript of Apocalyptic Artworks to Peruse at Will
items.desc: "The Book of Miracles," a 16th-century manuscript likely created in Augsburg, is heading to auction. It features 167 paintings of extreme weather events and strange celestial phenomena
items.text:
Ellen Wexler | Writer and Special Projects Editor
In the Bible, God’s will often emerges through natural phenomena. The great flood cleanses the earth of human corruption, while the rainbow symbolizes the divine covenant “between God and every living creature.” For millennia, worshippers familiar with these stories have wondered: What meaning can be found in the movements of storms, seas and stars?
That’s the central question of The Book of Miracles , an illustrated manuscript dating to the mid-16th century. Featuring 167 imaginative paintings, the text begins with episodes from the Old Testament and ends with apocalyptic visions from the Book of Revelation . Between them is a catalog of earthquakes , comet sightings , locust plagues , volcanic eruptions and other events spanning antiquity through the manuscript’s creation.
Now, The Book of Miracles is heading to the auction block, where it’s expected to fetch between roughly $920,000 and $1.3 million. Bidders can vie for the volume during Christie’s Valuable Books and Manuscripts sale on December 10.
“The artists of The Book of Miracles have reinterpreted historical and contemporary sources with apocalyptic panache,” per the lot listing . Illustrations of earthquakes, floods and other natural disasters that occurred in Europe are “among the most energetic, imaginative and colorful illustrations in the manuscript.”
The text was rediscovered in the library of a Bavarian castle about two decades ago. It’s since changed hands several times. After acquiring the manuscript, London art dealer James Faber helped date it to the 16th century. The publisher Taschen released a facsimile edition in 2013.
Because The Book of Miracles depicts about a dozen events near Augsburg , a city in modern-day Germany, scholars think it may have been created there. Christie’s attributes the manuscript to two painters, Hans Burgkmair the Younger and Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger , and their workshops. Nobody knows who commissioned the manuscript—or what exactly that individual had in mind. “Its existence was hitherto unknown, and silence wraps its discovery,” the New York Review of Books ’ Marina Warner wrote in 2014. “This Book of Miracles is a gorgeous unheralded surprise: a foundling of unknown parents, a virgin birth.”

items.text:
Pierre before cataract surgery at Chimp Haven.
The world’s largest chimpanzee sanctuary, Chimp Haven in Louisiana, has performed its first successful cataract removal operation on one of its residents.
Pierre the chimp has long been the alpha of his social group. So when keepers noticed him withdrawing, they knew he was having trouble with his eyesight, eventually going completely blind. Originally from a research laboratory in New York, Pierre had built a reputation as a friendly and inviting presence within his social group who was quick to welcome any newcomers and help them settle into the troop.
But as his cataracts progressed, his daily routines changed. Instead of spending time with the other chimpanzees, Pierre began keeping to himself. He stopped moving around as much and increasingly relied on his hands to feel his way through his surroundings. His caregivers initially suspected he was struggling with his vision, and over the next year he became completely blind.
Over that year, Chimp Haven's care team worked closely with Dr. Kenneth Pierce, a veterinary ophthalmologist, to determine whether Pierre was a suitable candidate for cataract surgery. Pierre passed every test with flying colors and was cleared for the procedure. The operation went well, and he proved to be an excellent patient throughout both surgery and recovery.
But the surgery was only one step in the healing process. Since regaining his eyesight, Pierre returned to climbing and moving around comfortably. He can once again recognize his caregivers and navigate his surroundings without relying on touch to guide him. After spending roughly a year unable to see, he also needed to reconnect with the chimpanzees in his social group.
Reintroduction went smoothly, and Pierre's troop was excited to see him back to his normal self. His caregivers have even noticed behaviors they had not seen from him in quite some time. He no longer carries the weight of being the group’s alpha male, giving him a chance to enjoy life without the demands of leading his troop. Pierre will continue to live his best life with his troopmates and caregivers to watch over him.

items.title: I want to know if toxic lagoon fire caused my husband's rare deadly cancer
items.desc: Steve Williams died of lung cancer 14 years after falling in to a lagoon at a toxic waste dump fire.
items.text:
Firefighter Steve Williams, pictured here with his widow Jilska, died of a rare lung cancer 14 years after falling into a toxic lagoon
It was a sight which struck terror into the firefighters called to tackle it - a blazing chemical waste lagoon on fire, with barrels exploding into the air.
Steve Williams, then in his 20s, was one of 60 firefighters sent to tackle the burning Llwyneinion lagoon in August 1980, which was sending thick black smoke over a nearby village.
Steve slipped in and, although he was pulled out, his widow thinks what he swallowed may have cost him his life from a rare form of lung cancer aged 39. She said "someone should be held accountable".
Wrexham council, which owns the site, said while it did not meet the legal definition of "contaminated land", it regularly inspected and monitored the area.
It took 60 firefighters about 18 hours to bring the 1980 fire at Llwyneinion lagoon under control
A leading expert in fire chemistry and toxicity said it was difficult to establish a link between firefighters' exposure to chemicals and health issues later in life.
Steve's widow Jilska Williams believes the father-of-two's terminal cancer could have stemmed from the chemicals at the fire at the former toxic waste dump near Wrexham in north Wales.
"It's a definite probability," said the 71-year-old. "They're firemen and they're always running into fires, so you don't know what the long-term effects are going to be - but actually falling into the lake and drinking that fluid, which is full of chemicals. He had a double-whammy, didn't he?"
Steve's family are part of a group which came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.
This is the last family photo of Jilska and Steve Williams, with their children David and Kelly, taken in June 1994, shortly before he was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer
They want surviving firefighters to be tested for deadly carcinogens they fear they were exposed to in the fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon.
Eleven firefighters or their families have told a BBC investigation about concerns the fire could have had an impact on their health.
They said there was an increased number of miscarriages suffered by partners of those who attended the fire in the year after - and also highlighted concerns about rates of cancers since.

What began as an exciting hiking trip quickly turned into something else entirely when climbers in Greece found an orphaned seal pup on a beach at the bottom of a cliff.
Considered a Critically Endangered species in Greece, the climbers resolved to go right back up the way they came—the seal pup safely secured in a backpack.
It was stranded without its mother on the inaccessible Kalamia Beach—whose beauty and solitude were supposed to be the climbers’ reward for negotiating the rugged cliffs on the island of Kythira.
Vrettos Sklavos, from Outdoor Activities Greece said there is a sea cave near Kalamia Beach that these Mediterranean monk seals use to escape rough seas. Perhaps a big wave had separated the little fellow from its mother.
An animal rescue operation on the island wrote on Facebook that the climbers took “all the right steps,” calling (MOm) the Hellenic Society for the Study and Protection of the Mediterranean Monk Seal, the coast guard, and Animal Aid Kythira , whose veterinarians eventually descended the cliffs together with the climbers to rescue the seal.
“A huge thank you to Vrettos and his team for their immediate response,” the operation wrote on Facebook.
In an update from Keep Talking Greece , the seal is said to have arrived severely dehydrated and malnourished, weighing just 15 kilograms at 1 year old. It was determined that after a brief stay with Animal Aid Kythira it would be transported to Thessaly on the mainland before eventually arriving at the Society’s rehabilitation location in Spata.
Here, it will receive round-the-clock care with the aim of attempting to preserve enough of its wild intuition and nature as to permit a return to the sea when the time is right.

2 prominent chemical compounds prohibited under international law over health concerns are being found at substantially lower concentrations in England’s rivers.
Concentrations of these so-called ‘forever chemicals’ falling 30% in water and 49% in fish was “brilliant to see,” one researcher told the BBC , saying it was a marker for “how far we have come.”
For many decades, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, have been used to create coatings that resist fire, oil, stains, and water. They’re used in products like waterproof clothing, stain-resistant furniture, food packaging, adhesives, cosmetics, firefighting spray foams, medical equipment, and non-stick cooking surfaces.
All that time, however, PFAS were making their way into the environment where because of their unique structure and characteristics, they substantially resist biodegradation, earning them the moniker ‘forever chemicals.’
Two forms of PFAS known as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid, (PFOS) were banned under the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants in almost all products.
The UK being a party to the convention, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010, and PFOA in 2020. France implemented bans of these two chemicals in certain products in January, while the US Environmental Protection Agency announced new drinking water testing regimes for 6 common PFAS in 2024.
Despite this 10 year disparity, concentrations of PFOA in England’s rivers had still fallen 29% compared to 30% for PFOS in the recent test work conducted by the UK Environment Agency (EA).

There are thousands of different PFAS manufactured around the world, but far fewer are used on a wide scale. The EA now routinely tests for 60 forms of PFAS in the country’s rivers, lakes, groundwater, estuaries, coastal waters, fish, and shellfish
The World Health Organization’s Int. Agency for Research on Cancer considers there to be “sufficient” evidence that PFOA is carcinogenic in humans, while research on PFOS suggests this compound is “possibly carcinogenic” in humans.

Neighbors and total strangers rallied around an 87-year-old woman with Parkinson’s Disease named Carole, raising more than $109,000 and proving she was much less alone than she thought. All it took was one person to take the time to check on the person who lived upstairs.
Carole had lived alone for years, with no family nearby, and was struggling through her day-to-day life without much if any assistance. On top of the tremors and mobility issues caused by her Parkinson’s disease, Carole was living very near the poverty line, surviving on Social Security, SNAP, and Medicaid benefits in an upstairs apartment in Culver City, Los Angeles.
That’s when Carole got a new downstairs neighbor. Heidi Widmer arrived in Culver City from Buffalo looking for a fresh start. She was initially disappointed and frustrated to find she had a noisy upstairs neighbor—a thumping sound that she said sounded like someone bowling carried on for weeks. “I was miserable because I barely got any sleep,” Widmer recalled.
Everything changed when Carole’s tremors caused her to spill the recycling she was trying to take out right outside Widmer’s door. It had taken Carole about 20 minutes just to get down the stairs with a walker. When Widmer came out and helped her clean up, Carole’s first words were, “Thank you so much. Are you my new neighbor? Am I too loud for you?”
Widmer realized her “loud neighbor” was really just someone trying to stay independent. “That was just such a humbling moment for me,” she said. “I’m like, no, baby girl, you’re not loud at all.”
Annoyance turned to compassion, and suddenly Carole was no longer alone. Widmer, who has always been a caregiver by nature, stepped in. She takes out the trash twice a week, cooks for Carole once a week (including homemade pierogies), and helps with cleaning. She contacted the landlord, who has since installed or replaced an air-conditioning unit, carpet, stove, fridge, and screen door.
She has also helped navigate medical benefits and paperwork. Carole had gone years without a real hot meal.

items.title: See Stunning Images of the Universe Captured by Europe's Euclid Space Telescope, Which Is Building the Biggest 3D Map of the Cosmos
items.desc: The 1.7 million gigabytes of data include more than 900 million galaxies, more than 60 million potential quasars and about 15,000 candidates of an elusive cosmic phenomenon that can help scientists understand dark matter and dark energy
items.text:
After roughly 13 months of scientific observations, the Euclid space telescope—built by the European Space Agency (ESA)—has released its first big batch of data. The observations cover an area of the sky roughly equal to 9,500 full moons as viewed from Earth, and that’s just a tiny portion of what the observatory will capture as it builds the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos.
The contents of the 1.7-million-gigabyte data drop, unveiled on November 12, are astounding. They include more than 900 million galaxies; more than 60 million potential quasars , the bright cores of faraway galaxies; and about 15,000 candidates of an elusive phenomenon called strong gravitational lensing , which can help shed light on a cosmic mystery: the dark universe.
Euclid launched in July 2023 to journey to a spot nearly one million miles from Earth called Lagrange Point 2 , joining NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. ESA’s instrument aims to investigate two mysterious, invisible things : dark matter, which acts as cosmic glue, and dark energy, thought to be behind the universe’s accelerating expansion. Scientists suspect that together, they make up 95 percent of the universe , but neither can be measured directly. That’s why scientists are excited about the thousands of strong gravitational lensing candidates in this batch of data.
Did you know? Another Lagrange Point 2 buddy
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is currently en route to the second Lagrange point, where it will search for exoplanets and help unravel the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy.
Gravitational lensing occurs when light from a distant galaxy gets distorted by a galaxy between it and the light detector—in this case, Euclid. The way the light gets warped around the obstacle allows researchers to indirectly investigate the dark universe.
“How strongly the light is bent tells us how much matter a galaxy contains, including invisible components like dark matter. With thousands of lenses, we can study how dark ​matter is spread through galaxies and understand how galaxies form and evolve over cosmic time,” Natalie Lines , an astrophysicist at the University of Portsmouth in England and Euclid team member, tells Reuters ’ Will Dunham.

Engelbart never received any royalties for the invention of the mouse, and later said “SRI patented the mouse, but they really had no idea of its value.” Some years later it was learned that they had licensed it to Apple Computer for something like $40,000.
Described in the patent application as an “X-Y position indicator for a display system”, it consisted of a wooden shell with two metal wheels, and was nicknamed the ‘mouse’ because the tail came out the end.
Engelbart wanted to focus his career on making the world a better place by harnessing the collective human intellect of all people to contribute to effective solutions. He reasoned that if you could dramatically improve how we do that, you’d be boosting every effort on the planet to solve important problems—and computers could be the vehicle for dramatically improving this capability.

items.desc: It follows years of debate over the alleged impacts on rivers in an area dubbed "poultry capital".
items.text:
The legal action against Natural Resources Wales landed in the High Court
River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.
River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.
It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital" .
NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".
The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.
The three farms are Neuadd Isaf, Rhosddu and Llanshay.
Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.
Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.
The three poultry units in Powys are located within river catchments including the River Wye
Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.
Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.
Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.
Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.
River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.

items.title: A Modern Forensic Investigation Reveals the Cause of Death of a 2,000-Year-Old Body Found in a Bog in Northern Ireland
items.desc: Archaeologists teamed up with a coroner to determine that the "Ballymacombs More Woman" was just 15 to 22 years old when she was beheaded in what seems to be an Iron Age ritual sacrifice
items.text:
After more than 2,000 years, authorities Northern Ireland are making major discoveries in gruesome cold case. A public inquest-style inquiry has determined the cause of death of an young woman from the Iron Age, whose body was recovered in a peat bog in 2023. A coroner’s investigation concluded that she was deliberately beheaded from behind with a bladed weapon.
Hosted at the Ulster Museum in Belfast, the proceeding synthesized findings from an international research consortium led by National Museums NI (NMNI). Although not a formal legal inquest, the hearing applied contemporary investigative standards to examine the evidence behind a death more than 20 centuries ago.
“Finds like this that are women are incredibly rare,” Hannah Crowdy , head of curatorial at NMNI, tells the BBC ’s Eve Rosato. “She’s the first of her kind in Northern Ireland at all. This helps us piece together a part of history that is quite mysterious. To honor her, it’s important to tell her story and bring that to the fore.”
The remains were unearthed in October 2023, when peat workers from Bulrush Horticulture uncovered human bones in Ballymacombs More outside Bellaghy in County Londonderry .
Subsequent excavations recovered further skeletal remains and a woven artifact, though no skull was found. Researchers initially thought the body was male and dubbed the individual “ Bellaghy Boy ,” before forensic testing revealed the remains belonged to a young woman between 15 and 22 years old. She was subsequently renamed the Ballymacombs More Woman.
A post shared by Ulster Museum (@ulstermuseum)
Using micro-CT scanning, digital mapping, 3D imaging and targeted analyses of preserved bone, hair, skin, nails and the woven textile, researchers from nine institutions gathered clues about her diet, health and physical appearance.
Cut marks on the woman’s neck appear to indicate that she was “intentionally decapitated in the bog,” Niamh Baker , NMNI’s curator of archaeology, tells the BBC.
The reason for this decapitation is unknown. “It may be that she falls into a pattern of ritual and sacrifice that took place across northwest Europe in the Iron Age period,” Baker explains, adding that comparable Iron Age male remains found in the Republic of Ireland have been linked to leadership positions.
“Was she a female sovereign?” Baker asks. “Or it may be that it was related to an agricultural or weather issue at the time.”

items.title: These Adorable Hatchlings Are From the U.S. West Coast's First Known Natural Sea Turtle Nests. Now, They've Returned to the Wild
items.desc: Two nests were spotted in September, and authorities moved the eggs to an aquarium to protect them from an incoming tropical storm. Over the weekend, dozens of hatchlings emerged and have now been released on the same beaches where they were found
items.text:
In September, authorities in California were baffled to find two sea turtle nests on their beaches—the first natural ones ever confirmed on the United States’ West Coast. Now, dozens of the eggs have hatched. Experts released the baby olive ridley turtles over the weekend, allowing the tiny creatures to begin their perilous journeys to adulthood.
The two nests were identified on Seal Beach and Huntington Beach in Orange County. Because a tropical storm was coming soon after the nests were found, biologists moved the more than 200 eggs to the Aquarium of the Pacific. The Ping-Pong ball-size spheres stayed in closed incubators under sand in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room, simulating their ideal natural conditions.
Aquarium staff first saw signs of hatching activity on November 12, when they noticed changes in the surface of the sand in the incubation container with the Seal Beach eggs, said Lance Adams , the aquarium’s veterinarian, during a press conference on November 14. The team spotted a depression and some cracks in the sand, indicating something was happening beneath it. The first turtle emerged the following day at around 7:15 p.m. Pacific time. Around two hours later, more of the baby turtles from the Seal Beach nest started popping out, resulting in 54 squirming critters.
“It kind of went from looking like very smooth beach sand to looking like an eruption of baby sea turtles,” Adams explained. It “was really exciting and very, very cute.” As of the press conference date, 50 eggs from the nest had not hatched. Experts do not know whether they’re viable, but they will continue monitoring the makeshift home.
The Seal Beach hatchlings were released in the same location where their nest had been, very early on Saturday morning, before the sun had risen, according to a social media post . That’s because baby turtles use moonlight to navigate toward the ocean. After reaching the water, hatchlings experience a “frenzy period” in which they swim continuously for 24 to 48 hours, according to the post. The energetic outburst is justified; experts estimate that only one in 1,000 olive ridley turtle hatchlings survive to adulthood, according to a statement .

Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA 's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.
The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.
The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe . The United States has lost its measles elimination status as cases surge to the highest levels in decades.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), an international public health agency for the Americas, has concluded that the U.S. no longer meets the criteria for measles elimination, according to the Wall Street Journal ’s Liz Essley Whyte and Jennifer Calfas.
“Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system,” Demetre Daskalakis , a former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), tells CNN ’s Brenda Goodman. “It shows cracks in our foundation. Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges.”
Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, meaning there had been no continuous spread of the disease for more than 12 months. However, in recent years, the highly contagious viral disease has made a comeback.

From a waterfall of fog to almighty storms and sunrises, the winners of the 2026 Weather Photographer of the Year competition have been announced.
The competition run by the Royal Meteorological Society in the UK attracted over 5,500 entrants from around the world, with the judges’ winners selected by an international panel of experts in weather, climate, and photography.
In addition, the public voted for their favorite via the Royal Meteorological Society website .
Francisco Bailón Rodríguez took 1st place with an image taken on Mallorca.
Photographed at dawn, looking towards the Formentor Peninsula, the image shows fog spilling over cliffs towards the sea. Humid nights and persistent high pressure helped the fog develop, while a southwesterly wind carried the low cloud across the rugged landscape. At first glance it becomes difficult to discern where the fog ends and the sea begins.
Runner-up was awarded to Weilu Chen, from China with a spectacular photograph of the Sun’s golden light over the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macao Bridge, with crepuscular rays fanning across the sky above the Pearl River Delta.
These striking beams appear as sunlight streams through gaps in the clouds, alternating with bands of shadow.
Third place was given to Laura Hedien, from the United States. Captured during a night-time storm chase, Hedien’s photograph freezes a lightning strike illuminating a supercell and the lake below.
The flash reveals a shelf cloud along the storm’s leading edge, formed as cool outflow lifts warmer, moist air ahead of it.
“A huge congratulations to all our winners and runners-up. The standard of the photographs submitted this year was incredibly high. These breathtaking images showcase the weather and climate in its pure beauty, complexity, and intensity,” said Professor Liz Bentley, Chief Executive of the Royal Meteorological Society.
In parallel to the judges’ decisions were the results of the public vote, which produced a different slate of winners led by Mahmudul Hasan, from Malaysia, with a breathtaking image of the tea-growing region of Long Coc in Vietnam.
At first light, layers of mist revealed the rounded hills in a wave-like pattern, creating a tranquil scene shaped by both weather and agriculture.
Public choice runner-up was awarded to Dan Martland, who captured a triple lightning strike over the skyline of New York City with the Statue of Liberty in the foreground.

How much sleep do you get each night? According to the National Center for Health Statistics , one-third of American adults sleep less than seven hours a night—the amount of shuteye recommended by health authorities. Recognizing that many people, particularly students, struggle to get the rest they need, researchers recently explored whether offering small, financial rewards could encourage students to improve their sleeping habits.
The study, published in July 2026, was conducted by Osea Giuntella, associate professor of economics at the University of Pittsburgh; Sally Sadoff, professor of economics and strategy at the University of California, San Diego; and Silvia Saccardo, professor of social and decision sciences at Carnegie Mellon University.
The researchers gave more than 1,100 undergraduates at University of Pittsburgh a Fitbit, a wearable activity tracker that recorded how much they slept, and an app that sent bedtime reminders and morning feedback. They randomly chose 468 freshman students and paid them around $5 for every night they slept at least seven hours over the course of four weeks.
Before the study, students at the University of Pittsburgh were getting an average of just 6.6 hours of sleep a night. “Half were going to bed after 1 a.m. on average—a quarter after 2 a.m,” reveal the researchers. “They also did not know how much sleep they were getting. Two-thirds told us they usually slept seven hours—the trackers showed only about one-third of students slept that much on even three nights out of five.”
Students offered money for getting enough sleep reached the seven hour target on 26% more nights than those who weren’t paid. They also got an extra 19 minutes of sleep each school night—about the difference between closing your laptop at 11:40 p.m. instead of midnight. Getting more sleep seemed to pay off in the classroom, too. Students who received the incentives saw their GPA rise by around 0.08 points that semester. The boost to grades didn’t last forever though, and lowered after two semesters.
The researchers also learned that students who were paid nightly slept more than those who received a lump sum at the end of the semester. Interestingly, bedtime reminders alone made little difference. Students already wanted more sleep—they just needed a little extra incentive to make it happen.

The “sensational” discovery of a cave containing the skeletons of over 100 extinct cave bears has been revealed by local authorities.
Kept secret to prevent looting, the incredible assemblage of thousands of bones will remain tucked away behind iron bars until the spring thaw when an interdisciplinary team of scientists will begin studying them.
Discovered in July by a mountain guide in the Autonomous Province of South Tyrol, northern Italy, the cave sits around 9,100 feet above sea level on the side of an almost sheer cliff.
The guide, Kurt Walde, found the cave in the municipality of Enneberg just above another famous cave called Conturines, the highest in altitude in which cave bear remains had ever been found.
That cave was tragically looted before scientists had a chance to study all the animals that lived and died there. When Walde discovered this new, potentially even greater trove of extinct animal bones, Director of the Archeological Heritage Office, Christian Terzer, began work to construct a metal gate and protective tarp over the cave entrance to prevent similar illegal incursions.
“The logistical challenges of managing this project on a vertical rock face at almost 3000 meters above sea level were enormous,” Terzer said in a government statement.

“With this safety operation, we are protecting not only an extraordinary site, but also the knowledge it contains. Now the scientific work begins, which will give us a more precise picture of how cave bears lived in the Dolomites,” added Provincial Councilor Philipp Achammer in the statement.
It’s unclear to scientists whether the cave hosted Ursus spelaeus or Ursus spelaeus ladinicus, two species of large bear known from Western Europe that lived during the Pleistocene, and which died out during the last Ice Age.
They were significantly larger than today’s brown bears, reaching more than 11 feet in length and standing 5.5 feet at the shoulder, yet they foraged almost exclusively on plant material. Sarah Blaffer Hrdy unpicked Darwinian sexism to rewrite the story of evolution. Now, she’s turned her attention to the nature of fatherhood
‘S pit here, dear,” Sarah Blaffer Hrdy said to her husband, Dan, handing him a vial when he arrived in New York after the birth of the couple’s first grandchild. It was 2014 and Hrdy was conducting an experiment. Having recorded a 63% jump in oxytocin in her saliva after spending hours cuddling the baby, she wanted to find out if something similar would happen to his hormones.
It did, although it took a day longer. In her latest book, Father Time: A Natural History of Men and Babies , Hrdy records with justified pride that “this was the first time anyone had demonstrated a bump in oxytocin levels among doting grandparents”.
The nurturing man, Hrdy says on a video call from her home in rural northern California, used to be laughed off as an “imaginary creature” by some of her colleagues. But “what we’re seeing in many developed countries is something very unusual for mammals that has astounded me as an evolutionary biologist – men completely committed to looking after babies with a tenderness that you think of as maternal”.
As well as higher levels of oxytocin, researchers have found lowered testosterone in fathers who care for babies – mirroring findings in other mammals and bird species. But neuroscientists have also learned something else. When they scanned the brains of men who were primary carers, neural circuits in the hypothalamus and amygdala were activated, rather than the much newer – in evolutionary terms – neocortex. What this suggested to Hrdy was that such men are drawing on a genetic inheritance shared with fish, frogs and other species in which paternal care features. Her hope is that the activation of such capacities could, over time, help to bring about a less belligerent world.
“This is the country where 40% of us elected a man who brags about never changing a diaper , and we’ve got Pete Hegseth [the secretary of defence], who says we need men with higher testosterone. Boy, do I have news for him. If you have normal testosterone and take supplements, your sperm count is going to go pishooo” – she demonstrates with a swooping downward gesture and laughs.

The teamLab Forest Fukuoka museum by Tokyo-based art collective teamLab is a one-of-a-kind space that invites you to immerse yourself in a digital wonderland. Opening Nov. 21, Catching and Collecting Extinct Forest is the collective’s latest interactive artwork. Its permanent installation features a mythical forest inhabited by various animals that respond to the actions of visitors.

Each creature is then added to their digital collection book, where they can learn more about it. Participants can also release animals back into the forest by swiping them towards a location on their screen. Rock layers record the Earth’s history, typically piling up from oldest at the bottom to youngest at the top. But a giant, mysterious gap exists in many of the globe’s landmasses. It’s well-documented in North America, northern Europe and northern China, where in some places more than one billion years of our planet’s geologic record is nowhere to be found.
Now, scientists say they may have figured out what caused the so-called Great Unconformity.
Computer simulations hint the missing rock layers, which should be older than roughly 540 million years old, were uplifted by movements of Earth’s viscous mantle layer and eroded away by giant ice sheets before the continents sank back down again. The findings, published November 4 in the journal Nature , help validate some of the possible explanations about the Great Unconformity, possibly solving the 150-year-old mystery.
“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. Researchers first described the Great Unconformity in the late 1800s in the layers of the Grand Canyon .

items.desc: Centuries ago, the Parthenon's east pediment was reduced to rubble. German researchers now believe they have recreated the 39-figure scene depicting the birth of Athena with the help of Roman sarcophagi and 3D printers
items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
When the Parthenon was built some 2,500 years ago atop the Acropolis of Athens, one of the temple’s facades stood out for its striking imagery. Stretching for nearly 100 feet above the building’s eastern entrance, the marble-carved pediment depicted Athena being birthed from the head of a nearly 13-foot-tall Zeus; they were flanked on either side by 37 other intricately sculpted figures, including gods and goddesses. For its fine craftsmanship and potent symbolism, the pediment is widely considered by scholars to be one of antiquity’s most famous images.
But no one alive today has ever looked upon the scene in its original glory. Sometime between the fifth century C.E. and 1670, the pediment was largely destroyed—fires, earthquakes and humans all played roles in its destruction. Only 20 percent of the ruins were recovered, and these fragments have since been scattered to museums across the world. Piecing together what the original artwork may have looked like has intrigued historians for centuries. Now, a team of researchers believe they have finally reached a solution to the Parthenon puzzle.
Open this week at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt, Germany, “ Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle ” offers visitors a chance to see what the institution is calling the first-ever “archaeologically grounded proposal” for what the pediment once looked like.
“For around 200 years, archaeological research has sought to reconstruct the lost overall appearance of the Parthenon’s east pediment,” Philipp Demandt , the museum’s director, says in a statement . “With this exhibition, we are presenting our findings to the public for the first time and inviting visitors to take a fresh look at and discuss one of the most significant works of art from antiquity.”

items.title: From a Small Island in Denmark, This Man Lived Through the Transition From Hunter-Gathering to Farming 6,000 Years Ago
items.desc: A new analysis of the Rødhals Man suggests he witnessed the Neolithic Revolution in his lifetime, growing up eating mostly foraged seafood before shifting to more land-based, likely farmed, foods as an adult
items.text:
Archaeologists have identified a man who likely lived through the shift from hunter-gathering to farming, a dramatic transition that reshaped human history and ultimately paved the way for modern society as we know it.
Researchers have uncovered new details about the diet, lifestyle and health of the “Rødhals Man,” an indigenous hunter-gatherer who lived some 6,000 years ago in what is now Denmark. The findings, published November 16 in the journal Antiquity , suggest the Rødhals Man witnessed the Neolithic agricultural revolution and seemingly found a way to co-exist with farmers.
Rødhals Man is the name given to a near-complete skeleton discovered in 1956 in a shell midden—essentially, an ancient trash dump—on the small Danish island of Sejerø .
For years, researchers were perplexed by the remains. Radiocarbon dating suggested the man was alive between 3900 B.C.E. and 3800 B.C.E., after Neolithic farmers had already begun arriving on the nearby island of Zealand , and lived during a time when people were starting to eat mostly land-based foods grown and raised by farmers. But his DNA revealed that his ancestry was entirely indigenous—he belonged to the Western Hunter-Gatherer genetic group—and his diet consisted primarily of seafood .
“There was something wrong and it is always when things don’t fit that you may be on the track of something important,” lead author Anders Fischer , an archaeologist at the University of Gothenburg, tells New Scientist ’s Chris Simms.
So, researchers decided to take another look at the remains. Their analysis revealed that the Rødhals Man was between 30 and 40 years old when he died—probably closer to the upper end of this range, based on degenerative changes to his body. In life, he stood roughly five feet tall and was right-handed. He had black hair and dark skin, and there’s a very high likelihood his eyes were blue.
The Rødhals Man shows no signs of having experienced violence, and he appears to have been healthy during the early part of his life. Later, as he aged, he developed inflammation or a vitamin deficiency.
An investigation of his teeth and bones revealed that his diet changed over the course of his life. As a child, he mostly ate creatures like mollusks, flatfish or eels, which he likely foraged from the shallow waters surrounding the island. Starting around age 11, however, he began to eat more land-based protein, in addition to seafood.

Antarctic blue whales have increased in number 1,000% since 1973 when the harpoons were finally hung up for good.
Growing from just 418 whales to 4,018, the superb recovery has averaged 4.5% per year.
Though the International Whaling Commission banned the killing of Antarctic blue whales in 1964, illegal whaling continued until 1973. These long-lived animals—the largest ever known to have existed—reproduce very slowly with just one calf every 3 years or so.
As impressive a comeback as the whales have made, counting 4,018 animals was also quite the impressive feat of data science.
Even though one can spot a blue whale with a satellite, the Southern Ocean population spends most of its time underwater.
Zoe Rand, a postdoctoral scholar in the University of Washington School of Marine and Environmental Affairs, lead a study that examined historical catch data, modern photo identification records, and decades of “line transect” surveys to estimate current population.
Line transect surveys from 1978 to 1984, 1985 to 1991, and 1991 to 2004 surveyed the entire Southern Ocean by sailing boats along straight lines and counting whales seen and the distances they remained from the boat.
These data sources not only indicated the number was growing, but that it has grown so substantially over time.

Animals have always been an endless source of entertainment. Whether they’re racing around the house like they’ve lost their minds or dozing off with their little paws tucked under their chins, we never seem to get tired of watching them. Sometimes, though, their behavior can leave us scratching our heads .
It would be nice to ask them directly about their strange habits, but it’s not like they can talk back. Luckily, scientists have spent years studying these creatures and have come up with some pretty interesting explanations for the things they do.
Take cats , for example. If you’ve ever watched one deliberately push a glass off a table, you might have wondered what it was trying to accomplish. According to PetMD , this behavior is often linked to their natural curiosity and hunting instincts.
Cats use their paws to investigate unfamiliar objects, and seeing how something moves or reacts can be quite interesting to them. They also enjoy attention from their humans, so if they realize that knocking things over gets them noticed, they might make a habit of it.
Another animal quirk that might seem strange but hilarious to us humans is the good old zoomies. As many pet owners know, cats and dogs can suddenly start sprinting around the house as if they’re competing in an Olympic race.
This behavior actually has a scientific name: frenetic random activity periods, or FRAPs. But why does it happen? According to experts from the University of Adelaide , these episodes can happen when animals are excited or releasing pent-up energy after a period of rest or inactivity. Maybe we should give it a try ourselves sometime!
Rabbits do something similar to the zoomies, although their version looks a little different. Sometimes, they’ll suddenly leap into the air and twist their bodies as though they’re performing an acrobatic stunt.
This behavior is known as a “binky,” and according to the RSPCA , it’s a sign that a rabbit is feeling happy and excited. So if you ever see one doing this, it’s simply jumping for joy!

This week the Empire State Building was illuminated in gold to celebrate NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft passing one light-day away from Earth.
It now takes the farthest man-made object from Earth 24 hours to send a signal back to NASA headquarters.
“The color gold is emblematic of the gold-plated copper phonograph record that is flying on Voyager,” NASA wrote on Tuesday. “The record contains sounds and images selected to portray the diversity of life and culture on Earth.”
The 12-inch gold-plated copper disc is intended as a message from humanity to any civilization that may encounter it. It includes 115 images, natural sounds, music from different cultures and eras, and spoken greetings in 55 languages.
Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 to study Jupiter and Saturn. It crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and continues to send data back to Earth nearly 50 years after its launch.
On Wednesday, the spacecraft passed one light-day from Earth: the distance light travels in 24 hours, or about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).
NASA will be celebrating the milestone today because of the very fact that it will take one day to receive the signal sent on Wednesday.
For its part, Voyager seems to have decided to celebrate by relaying that it has a problem: something it has been wont to do of late; though considering its age and the distance it has traveled, it can hardly be surprising.
It was on Tuesday that the Voyager 1 mission team became aware that the spacecraft had stopped sending science and engineering data, though ground-based antennae were able to find its carrier signal.
The presence of a carrier signal means that Voyager 1’s Attitude and Articulation Control computer is doing its job to keep the spacecraft pointed at Earth and that its antenna, as well as its broadcast equipment, still work. The lack of data suggests the issue is with the onboard computer responsible for collecting the data from the spacecraft’s various subsystems, including science instruments, and putting it into the right format to be transmitted to Earth.
GNN has previously reported on the vagaries involved with trying to keep a machine operational 15 billion miles away, and NASA’s team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory have had to come up with several creative solutions. By March 2024 , Voyager had had almost all of its instruments deactivated to save power.

Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves
Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering.
Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home.
Today, 18 November, that intrepid traveler – Voyager 1 , a robotic space probe the size of a Mini Cooper – is exactly one light day away from us: 16.1bn miles.
No other human-made object has ever gone this far. Radio signals from Earth (traveling at the speed of light, 186,000 miles per second ) now take 24 hours to reach it, and another 24 hours to return. The return signals are so weak that scientists at Nasa’s Deep Space Network must use a massive satellite dish to hear them.
Nasa launched Voyager 1 in early September 1977, just weeks after the first Star Wars movie hit theaters with Luke Skywalker and his charming sidekick droid, R2D2. It took photos of the planets Jupiter and Saturn , then continued onward.
In 2012 it exited the sun’s protective shield of charged particles and magnetic fields, crossed a boundary called the heliopause , and entered interstellar space. That’s when it became a message in a bottle.
That message consists of a 12in, gold-plated copper disk engraved with information to showcase human culture and the diversity of life on Earth, should any advanced civilization discover it. The disk contains photos and greetings in 55 human languages, music by Mozart and Chuck Berry, the sound of a baby crying and a whale singing. It also has a time stamp and a map that orients the position of our solar system to 14 pulsars – dense remnants of massive stars – that rotate rapidly and emit beams of radiation like flashing cosmic lighthouses. The message says, in essence: this is where we live and who we are. We thrive on connection. Come see us sometime.

items.text:
Capri, Italy, boasts dramatic cliffs, bright blue waters, and sunny Mediterranean weather, making it one of the most alluring tourist destinations in the world. However, this idyllic site has recently made waves around the world for a completely different reason. A double waterspout appeared next to one of Capri’s main attractions, and this rare weather phenomenon was captured on video.
The clip, captured by Massimo Aprea, shows the two swirling columns almost intertwining over the iconic Faraglioni rock formations. The result is a near-optical illusion of a delicate gray arch framing the landscape. Upon closer inspection, one can see the two parallel water pillars descending from the stormy sky and touching the ocean.
A waterspout is a whirling column of air and water mist, as winds blowing from opposite directions slam into each other. In this particular case, cooler winds moved over the warm Mediterranean air as a storm approached. This created localized areas of spinning air on the water’s surface.
Waterspouts are divided into two categories, fair weather waterspouts and tornadic waterspouts. The double one seen in Capri falls onto the latter, meaning they have the same characteristics as a land tornado, and they are usually accompanied by severe thunderstorms, as well as high winds and seas, large hail, and frequent dangerous lightning.
While the double watersprout provided a beautiful natural spectacle, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) says these type of watersprouts can quickly become dangerous, so it’s best to stay out of their way.
“The best way to avoid a waterspout is to move at a 90-degree angle to its apparent movement,” the NOAA states. “Never move closer to investigate a waterspout. Some can be just as dangerous as tornadoes.” The agency adds that if a waterspout moves onshore, the National Weather Service will issue a tornado warning.

items.text:
Olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings saved from an approaching storm in California were released into the wild over the weekend.
It was late September when a female turtle climbed out of the sea, dug a nest on the beach, deposited her clutch, and slipped back into the water leaving nothing but a small trail in the sand and a couple of speechless lifeguards.
This first-ever instance of a turtle nesting on America’s Pacific coast was repeated a day later on Huntington Beach in what were the first ever recorded sea turtle nests on the West Coast.
After at first being left to incubate and hatch naturally, storm forecasts saw state and federal authorities evacuate the nests and take the eggs to the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach.
The hatchlings emerged at the Aquarium and were quickly transported to Orange County beaches for release. Photos released by the Aquarium that were taken with red or infrared light show handlers measuring each hatchling before letting them scurry down to the water on their own, with minimal human disturbance and other distractions.
“It is not known why these sea turtles chose Southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it may indicate important historical changes that could have long-term implications for this species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” said Cassandra Davis, Director of Volunteer Services at the Aquarium, who said neither weather nor mere anomalous behavior were being ruled out as a theory.
Jonathan Snyder of the US Fish and Wildlife Service office in Carlsbad said another nest was recently documented further up the coast in Ventura County in November, and that it’s therefore unclear exactly how many turtles have nested in total.
He told reporters that one obvious potential reason for this never-before-witnessed event could be the Super El Niño weather phenomenon this year, though his overarching thoughts were positive.
“There have been decades of effort by dedicated individuals both in the US and abroad that have done everything they can for sea turtle conservation, and those efforts have really moved the needle for conservation for a variety of species, but for Olive Ridley sea turtles in particular,” said Snyder in a press conference.
“Their populations have increased substantially throughout portions of their range, and it’s the reason why there are these sea turtles along our coast that could take advantage of these unique environmental conditions.”

items.title: Europe's Hera Spacecraft Has Begun Its Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid System NASA Intentionally Hit in 2022
items.desc: The European Space Agency's mission will provide valuable data about the aftermath of the planned collision, which can inform planetary defense measures and reveal insights about asteroids
items.text:
The European Space Agency (ESA) has started its close-up investigation of an asteroid system smashed by NASA in 2022.
ESA’s Hera spacecraft reached the Didymos binary asteroid system on November 4, more than two years after it launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The mission will examine the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) collision, helping scientists better understand how the technique could one day be used to protect Earth from incoming space rocks.
The asteroid Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet in diameter and has a companion moonlet called Dimorphos, which is about 495 feet in diameter. They form a binary asteroid system , a pair of asteroids that are gravitationally bound, orbiting each other around a shared center of mass.
In September 2022, the golf-cart-size DART spacecraft intentionally struck the smaller celestial body in the world’s first demonstration of asteroid deflection technology. The mission not only successfully collided with Dimorphos, shortening its orbit around its big sibling by 33 minutes; it also altered the asteroid pair’s route around the sun . Now, Hera is returning to the crash scene to follow up on that work.
“Hera wants to be the detective, like Inspector Colombo, going back to the crash scene,” Patrick Michel , a planetary scientist at the French National Center for Scientific Research and Hera’s principal investigator, tells Meghan Bartels for Space.com .
The spacecraft, which is about the size of a small car , performed its first arrival maneuver on October 15, and ESA released Hera’s first close-up photo of the asteroid duo on November 5. The picture, snapped about 37 miles from the rocky pair, prominently features Didymos, with the smaller Dimorphos mostly hidden in the larger asteroid’s shadow.
While looking at this image, “the first thing we said was wow!” Michel says in a statement . “This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.”
On November 12, ESA released another image of the asteroid system , this time taken from about 35 miles away. It shows one side of Didymos and a sliver of Dimorphos peeking out from behind the larger rock, on the upper left. This photo reveals various features on the bigger asteroid’s surface, including large boulders, smooth areas and a sharp ridge at the equator.

Georgia O'Keeffe, “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I,” 1930. (Photo: Christie’s Images Ltd. )
You never know what could be hiding in someone’s closet. Earlier this year, a long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting was discovered in the closet of a woman’s Manhattan apartment, and was recently presented as part of Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale in New York.
The 1930 painting, Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I , was estimated to be worth between $3 million and $5 million. On Nov. 17, it sold at auction for $4.8 million. It depicts the tan, green, and brown rolling mountains of New Mexico, using O’Keeffe’s signature sweeping curves that bring the viewer’s eye across the landscape. O’Keeffe first visited New Mexico in 1929 and it would continue to inspire her to paint throughout her career.
“This is a wonderful painting, a remarkable story, and extraordinary opportunity for collectors and the general public alike,” said Tylee Abbott, senior specialist and international director of American Art at Christie’s.
The discovery of the painting itself was just as remarkable. The owner of the work, who wished to remain anonymous, had invited her niece to her East Village apartment earlier this year to help go through her belongings. While the niece knew that her aunt was an art collector, she was shocked when the woman casually mentioned that she had an O’Keeffe in her front closet.
After digging through the closet, her niece found an old wooden box tucked behind dozens of coats. Inside was the 10-inch by 24-inch painting, complete with O’Keeffe’s signature on the original backboard. The painting had been a graduation gift to the owner when she earned her master’s degree in the 1960s. It was purchased by her mother for just $3,800 from O’Keeffe’s art dealer in Manhattan.
The painting hung on the wall of her apartment for over 20 years, until the owner grew worried after noticing that a guest was paying a little too much attention to it. She decided to tuck it away in its original box in the closet, where it remained hidden for decades.
Now, after spending decades out of sight, the painting is finally getting to see the light of day. The work was on public display at Christie’s New York, November 7-17, ahead of its appearance at the auction house’s 20th Century Evening Sale.

items.text:
From the sun-soaked plains of Parma comes the story of an Italian farmer who accidentally brought on a Biblical resurrection with very modern implications for our food system.
Claudio Grossi doubted whether the shriveled wheat seeds he found in his attic would grow into anything.
Grossi threw the seeds into a pile of manure, curious to see what might come of it. Soon, he found wheat stalks that towered over his commercial wheat crop, and instead of sprouting one ear, these stalks sprouted seven.
The pattern of those 7 ears proved important. One tall ear was surrounded by 6 thin ears of different colors. Grossi had spent his whole life farming wheat and had never heard of anything like it.
Smithsonian Magazine’s Lina Zeldovich wrote that he could find nothing about it in any agricultural manuals, a clue as to the “freak” grain’s origin did indeed come from a Good Book.
“And behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good,” read a page in the Book of Genesis that Grossi happened upon one Sunday in church. 7 ears, one stalk, just like the “freak of nature” at his farm.
Indeed, what his great-grandfather grew after he bought the farm in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region in 1915 was an ancient form of wheat called Triticum turgidum convar. compositum, as scientists at the University of Parma would later determine. It evolved in Türkiye, Egypt, and other countries along the Mediterranean, and was cultivated one upon a time in Italy.
As a commercial grain, its production declined around the time of the Mussolini dictatorship because its impressive height made it vulnerable to snapping under wind, heavy rains, and hailstorms before the grains would mature.
Additionally, dough made from T. turgidum flour doesn’t leaven well, and unusual preparations need to be made for baking with it.
Yet one by one, the positives which Grossi experienced made him wonder why Italian farmers ever stopped cultivating it. Tall, large, and hardy, it overshadows weeds, shows resistance to drought, and appears less reliant on fertilizer than other breeds. Grossi began calling it his “Miracle Wheat” or grano del miracolo.

items.text:
Huge strides were made for the Land Back movement on Cape Cod. On October 30, 2026, approximately 126 acres of ancestral land were returned to Indigenous ownership. Given the history of the land itself, the transfer was a particularly meaningful one, more than 400 years in the making.
The land, which overlooks what is now known as First Encounter Beach in Eastham, Massachusetts, is near where the Nauset, who are part of the Wampanoag Nation, first came across a group of Pilgrims who had arrived aboard the Mayflower in 1620. While the name of the beach commemorates this historic encounter, it was also the site of a confrontation in which the Nauset defended their homeland.
The property had been in the care of The Nature Conservancy since 1986 and was recently gifted to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit organization based in Mashpee, a historic town located on the Upper Cape. Founded in 2012, the organization works to preserve natural landscapes while reconnecting Indigenous communities with their ancestral lands.
“This location holds so many stories that were buried and are ready to be unearthed,” said Ramona Peters, founder and board president of the Native Land Conservancy and a member of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe.
Earlier this year, the organization also purchased a neighboring 20.4-acre property, meaning that approximately 146 acres of land in the area are now under Indigenous care. The conservation area has been given the name T8nupâhs Uwatuhshât, which translates to “at the turtle’s nest” in Wôpanâak. The name is particularly fitting, as diamondback terrapins return to the area each year to lay their eggs.
Aside from its historical and cultural significance, the land is also home to a variety of wildlife, including the diamondback terrapin and eastern box turtle. The Native Land Conservancy will continue to protect the area’s natural habitats while providing Indigenous communities with an opportunity to reconnect with the land and its history.

items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
Since it was announced last month that a celebrated Frida Kahlo painting would be put up for auction at Christie’s highly anticipated 20th Century Evening Sale , excitement and intrigue had steadily built.
Experts estimated that Kahlo’s 1952 Congreso de los pueblos por la paz ( Congress of the Peoples for Peace ), would fetch between $2.5 million and $3.5 million, a 52 percent increase from its most recent sale just six years ago. The piece shared the pre-auction spotlight with other high-profile works, including a Wassily Kandinsky masterpiece , a Gustav Klimt canvas and a long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe landscape that was recently rediscovered in a Manhattan closet .
But this week, just hours before the first bids were set to be submitted, Kahlo’s painting was pulled from the sale amid questions of its provenance. The interceding effort was led by a group called Defendamos la Colección Gelman (Let’s Defend the Gelman Collection), which seeks to protect Mexico’s cherished cultural artifacts from illegally leaving the country.
In a statement issued this week, the group says that the painting was included in a 1957 inventory that Kahlo’s husband, the famed painter Diego Rivera , created for the Casa Azul Trust, which left thousands of the pair’s artworks, artifacts and personal items to the Mexican people. The group goes on to allege that the work “left the Casa Azul for strange reasons and came into the hands of a New York gallery owner, and after several transfers and an auction it ended up in private hands that are now offering it, through Christie’s, for between $2 million and $3.5 million,” El País ’ Beatriz Guillén reports.

items.title: Giant lunar sculpture has visitors over the moon
items.desc: People can see the 6m-wide sculpture in St Helier until 29 November.
items.text:
The Moon sculpture is hanging at the St Helier Methodist Centre
People visiting a large illuminated sculpture of the Moon have said it is an "amazing" sight.
ArtHouse Jersey has brought Luke Jerram's artwork to the St Helier Methodist Centre until Sunday 29 November.
The 6m (20ft) wide display, which has been shown around the world, features detailed imagery of the lunar surface from photographs by Nasa.
Arthouse CEO Tom Dingle said: "Something that makes the most of a public space, that makes us think about the world around us, about ourselves, but also something that we can all share together all at once, is really exciting."
Eva, nine, said it was "cool" to see a sculpture of the Moon up close
The Moon follows a similar public artwork display in Jersey in 2023, when more than 31,000 people visited the Floating Earth on Queen's Valley Reservoir .
The installation features light and sound displays, which ArtHouse said would allow people "to encounter our closest celestial neighbour in an entirely new way".
Nine-year-old Eva thought the moon was "cool" and "like a big spot in the middle of the sky".
Primrose Keenan also enjoyed the exhibit, saying it was "amazing".
"We saw the Earth on the lake as well a few couple of years ago and that was amazing too," she added.
Toby Balderson said: "It does make a difference being able to see everything in such detail.
"We always just see little snapshots of it."
Youngsters Aquila and Starla, who are sisters, said it looked "really good" and "very big".
Dingle added: "Sometimes to stop, to take a pause and to reflect on the wider things, to think about the world out there, is actually really healthy and therapeutic."
He said the exhibit also showed the importance of free public artwork: "It enlivens our public realm, it gives us something to do together.
"It actually can change the pace for a day. It can give somebody a moment to reflect and it can mean something different to everybody - and yet we have the same universal experience at the same time."

items.text:
The North Atlantic right whale population shrank slightly in 2025, raising concerns about the future of the critically endangered species.
Scientists counted 382 individuals last year, according to new numbers released this week by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. That’s a 1.8 percent decrease from the 2024 estimate of 389 whales.
Meanwhile, the number of reproductive females held steady at 73, according to the consortium, which is made up of scientists from the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
North Atlantic right whales are massive marine mammals that can weigh as much as 140,000 pounds. They spend their winters in the shallow waters off North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, where they give birth and raise their calves. Then, they swim more than 1,000 miles north to spend the spring, summer and fall feeding in the food-rich waters off New England and Canada.
They’re one of three species of right whales, along with the North Pacific right whale and the Southern right whale . All three species are what’s known as filter feeders, meaning they use their baleen —flexible, comb-like plates that hang from their upper jaws—to tiny creatures called copepods from the water.
Commercial whalers hunted right whales to the brink of extinction by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, dubbing them the “right” whales to go after because they were relatively easy to kill and retrieve.
All three species have been protected under the U.S. Endangered Species Act since 1970. Still, the colossal creatures have been slow to recover—and their populations remain small today. Right whales can die or suffer life-threatening injuries after being struck by boats or becoming tangled in fishing gear.
“Imagine if you were wrapped in rope that moved as you moved … literally sawing into your body,” Philip Hamilton , a biologist with the New England Aquarium, tells CBC News ’ Leila Beaudoin. “It is really painful. They don’t have arms. The pain is … kind of unimaginable.”
Climate change, noise pollution and oil and gas development also threaten the whales. Rising ocean temperatures are particularly dangerous for the massive animals. As the North Atlantic heats up, copepods are moving toward cooler waters, prompting the whales to follow them into areas where they’re not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.

items.desc: The new theory about the "Arnolfini Portrait" comes as London's National Gallery brings together all 10 of the artist's known portraits for the first time ever
items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
Ahead of a new exhibition celebrating the portraiture of famed Netherlandish painter Jan van Eyck , a new theory has emerged about one of the artist’s most famous—and deeply puzzling—canvases.
At first glance, the scene in van Eyck’s 1434 Arnolfini Portrait seems straightforward: A man, dressed in black, and woman, clad in green, stand at the center of a lavish room where every detail—furniture, a dog, jewelry, oranges—is placed as though to purposefully highlight their wealth. But a closer look at the space’s geometry offers more uncanny observations. There is no fireplace, as would have been expected, and the ceiling is too low to realistically accommodate the chandelier that nonetheless dangles above their heads. Meanwhile, a convex mirror on the far back wall reveals that the pair are not alone; two figures are entering the room. The man in black lifts his hand, apparently in silent greeting, while a large inscription beside his head reads, in Latin: “Jan van Eyck was here 1434.”
Of all the details in the piece, which borders on the surreal, the identity of the man has been speculated upon the most. The leading theory derives from the 16th century, when inventory records labeling the painting as “hernoul le fin” were interpreted to be the French spelling of “Arnoul fin,” or “Arnolfini,” the surname of a wealthy Italian merchant clan who lived and worked in Bruges, Belgium, where van Eyck kept his studio.
For centuries, many art historians have supported this understanding, considering the piece to be a portrait of some members of that family. Some scholars identify the man as Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini, while others think it depicts his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini. But now, as London’s National Gallery prepares to open “ Van Eyck: The Portraits ,” an exhibition, a new theory put forth about the canvas potentially turns its meaning on its head.
Writing in the exhibition catalogue , Stephan Kemperdick , a curator at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie , posits that the painting is actually a self-portrait of van Eyck and his wife. His evidence is multi-faceted. He points to the Latin inscription as a clear self-reference and suggests that “hernoul le fin” actually translates to mean something like “a deceived cheat.” He argues that the painting, in the early modern period, would have been received as more of a lewd genre piece than a portrait. items.title: This Philosopher Was One of the First People to Donate His Body to Science. Nearly 200 Years Later, Researchers Are Still Learning From It
items.desc: Jeremy Bentham, the founder of utilitarianism, had his corpse publicly dissected and turned into an "auto-icon," a lifelike display featuring his skeleton dressed in one of his suits
items.text:
As a young man, English philosopher Jeremy Bentham vowed to donate his body to science, becoming one of the first people on record to make such a declaration. And he made good on his promise. After Bentham died at age 84, his remains were publicly dissected, then transformed into an “ auto-icon ”—a lifelike display featuring his skeleton dressed in one of his suits, which has been preserved by the University College London (UCL) ever since.
Now, nearly two centuries later, Bentham’s body is still yielding new scientific insights.
UCL researchers recently revisited Bentham’s remains, using computed tomography (CT) scanning to create a detailed, 3D model of his mummified head. They share the process and their findings in a short film called Bentham Revealed .
Born in 1748 in London, Bentham was a precocious child who enrolled at Oxford University at just 12 years old. Though he trained as a lawyer, he ultimately devoted his life to philosophy and writing. Bentham became best known as the founder of utilitarianism , a philosophy built around the idea that the best actions are those that produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people.
He applied this principle to a wide range of issues, advocating for prison reform , animal welfare , women’s rights , the decriminalization of homosexuality and the abolition of slavery—positions that were considered radical in 18th- and 19th-century Britain. His ideas inspired the founding of UCL, which opened to students in 1826.
But perhaps Bentham’s most radical act was his decision to donate his body to science. In his will, he bequeathed his corpse to his friend, British physician Thomas Southwood Smith , and asked him to arrange a public dissection of his body. Smith obliged, tasking anatomist Richard Dugard Grainger with carrying out the procedure five days after Bentham’s death in June 1832, according to a university statement . Smith then created the auto-icon, which he kept at his house until 1850, when he donated it to UCL. It’s currently on view at UCL’s student center.
Bentham coined the term auto-icon himself, defining it as “self image” or “self representation.” He hoped to inspire others to follow suit. “He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around,” Tannis Davidson , who led the recent research and serves as a curator at UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, tells Live Science ’s Tom Metcalfe.

items.title: How Did Ancient Egypt's Sacred Cats Live? More Than 100 Unwrapped Mummies Reveal Poor Living Conditions, Infections and Violence Before Death
items.desc: Osteological and chemical tests on 131 museum specimens reveal that domestic cats and wild-caught jungle cats later destined for mummification suffered high rates of disease and physical trauma
items.text:
Across ancient Egypt, millions of cats were once mummified and laid to rest in sprawling animal necropolises to honor the gods. Now, a closer look at more than a hundred preserved skulls reveals that these sacred animals endured surprisingly brutal lives.
Researchers analyzed 131 well-preserved cat skulls housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna that originally came from Beni Hassan , an ancient animal funerary site in Egypt’s Nile Valley, some 155 miles south of Cairo. The majority of skulls belonged to adult cats, mostly domestic and some wild. They were largely dated between 380 B.C.E. and 40 B.C.E Osteological and chemical examinations revealed widespread signs of gum disease, infections, healed wounds and fatal skull fractures, according to a study recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science .
“What struck us most was the high proportion of injuries and evidence of disease, suggesting that these cats lived in poor conditions,” Bea De Cupere , study co-author and archaeozoologist at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, tells Phys.org ’s Sandee Oster. “This is not what one would expect for animals destined to become votive mummies.”
In ancient Egypt, cats were revered as earthly embodiments of the goddess Bastet and frequently appeared on tomb walls and artifacts. Eventually, devotees began mummifying felines as sacred offerings across at least 20 animal cemeteries in Egypt, according to the study.
In the 19th and early 20th centuries C.E., however, excavators were mostly interested in human mummies and used ancient animal remains as ship ballast, fuel, fertilizer or powdered medicine. The Beni Hassan skulls—the largest known museum collection of ancient Egyptian cat skulls with documented origin—survived only because British biologist William A. Herdman salvaged a small portion of roughly 200,000 animal mummies set out for a fertilizer auction in Liverpool in 1890, according to Gizmodo ’s Gayoung Lee. Since 19th-century scientists were mainly interested in skulls, the cats’ torsos were likely discarded after unwrapping.

items.title: Oil firm fined for breaking environmental rules hundreds of times
items.desc: Ten charges involved oil, cyanide and other pollutants entering local waterways.
items.text:
Stanlow Oil Refinery, owned by Essar Energy, is the second largest refinery in Britain
One of the UK's largest oil refinery operators has been ordered to pay £873,473 after breaching environmental permit limits nearly 500 times over three years.
The Environment Agency (EA) said the Stanlow refinery in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, exceeded wastewater discharge limits at least 489 times between 2018 and 2020. Essar Oil (UK) Limited pleaded guilty to 12 charges in March .
Essar Oil, which trades as EET Fuels, was fined £800,000 and ordered to pay £73,473 in costs at Warrington Magistrates' Court.
EET Fuels said it regretted the "historic incidents" and had invested more than £24m to improve environmental performance.
Ten charges related to wastewater discharges containing oil, suspended solids and chemicals, including cyanide, into Thornton Brook, the River Gowy and the Manchester Ship Canal.
Two other charges concerned incidents in 2019.
The Manchester Ship Canal runs for 36 miles from Eastham in Wirral to Salford
In February 2019, between 15 and 20 tonnes of a chemical leaked into the ship canal after a vent was left open and a written procedure was not followed.
A month later, a contractor's vehicle ruptured an effluent pipe. During repairs, about 15 tonnes of partially treated sewage entered Thornton Brook, which leads to the protected Mersey Estuary.
Environment Agency officers reported a sheen of oil on local waterways, while vegetation downstream of the refinery's discharge point was blackened by oil in January 2020.
The company was fined £80,000 for each of the 10 offences, with no additional penalty for the two 2019 incidents. Three breaches from 2022 and 2023 were taken into consideration without further punishment.
Nigel Glasgow, the Environment Agency's area environment manager, said the case showed "a repeated failure to comply" with permit conditions.
An EET Fuels spokesperson said: "We take our environmental responsibilities extremely seriously and regret these historic incidents."
The company said its investment included rerouting wastewater to United Utilities' Ellesmere Port treatment works, resulting in "a significant improvement in environmental performance", including fewer discharges and reduced freshwater use.
